title: Don’t leave your leadership development to chance
author: Nick Hart
summary: Following a post arguing that leadership expertise differs from leadership experience and that development can be a lottery, Nick Hart asks what school leaders can do to take charge of their own growth. He describes two kinds of work: finding harder problems inside a familiar domain, and deliberately expanding into new ones. In familiar domains the tools are structured reflection on a decision or incident, Peter Senge's systems-thinking iceberg, and regular debriefs while memory is fresh. For disruptive experiences he suggests a scaffold of prompts such as zooming out and back in, slowing down, and asking someone who will see it differently. In new domains, leaders can take on new responsibilities, build relationships outside their area or visit other schools. He acknowledges limits from confidence, time, cognitive load and relationships, and previews a next post on making this systematic.
points: Leaders can do two kinds of development work: find harder problems in a known domain, or deliberately move into new domains.
A regular debrief after a significant decision or hard week, held before the memory fades, deepens reflection and exposes assumptions.
A short set of prompts, such as zoom out then in, slow down, and consult someone who sees it differently, can scaffold learning in the moment.
New responsibilities, relationships outside your area and visits to other schools each play a different role in widening a leader's thinking.
Confidence, time, cognitive load and relationships limit what individuals can do alone, which is why development needs to be made systematic.
quotes: Even when school context and social networks may seem outside of our control, what we do within them certainly is.

I see individuals as being able to do two kinds of work: continuing to find harder problems inside a domain you already know and deliberately expanding thinking into new domains. The first involves reflection and seeking out alternative views from people already close to you.
Practically, this means building in a regular debrief after a significant decision or a difficult week and being honest about what you’d do differently before the memory fades.
Working with other leaders on a shared problem tends to create the first condition. But it only works if you actually want it to change your thinking.

If you don’t have those connections, or you’re not convinced the opportunity is there for you, you can still build yourself a scaffold; a few prompts to reach for in the moment a disruptive experience arrives.
Seeking out a new responsibility is the deep end: chairing a working group outside your usual area, covering a colleague’s role for a term, volunteering for a project.

No leader can guarantee working in a context where they’ll experience situations to develop their hidden leadership knowledge but they can guarantee getting more out of the experiences available to them.
